What distinguishes a microcontroller from an application processor?
column2: A microcontroller integrates the core, flash, SRAM, clocks, reset and peripherals on one die, runs bare metal or an RTOS with no MMU-based OS, and is built for deterministic response, low power and low cost.

column1: Name the main regions of the Cortex-M default memory map.
column2: Code from 0x0000 0000 (flash, vector table), SRAM at 0x2000 0000, peripherals at 0x4000 0000–0x5FFF FFFF, external RAM and devices above, and the core's private peripheral bus (NVIC, SysTick, SCB, MPU, debug) at 0xE000 0000.

column1: How many flash wait states does a clock \(f\) need with access time \(t_{acc}\)?
column2: \(\text{WS} = \lceil f\,t_{acc}\rceil - 1\) (at least 0), from \((1 + \text{WS})/f \ge t_{acc}\). Each wait state buys a band \(1/t_{acc}\) wide.

column1: Give the first-order CPI model for code running from flash.
column2: \(\text{CPI} \approx \max(1, (1 + \text{WS})s/L) + b\,m\,\text{WS}\): a sequential term if the line is too narrow, plus WS stall cycles per taken branch whose target misses.

column1: Why can a clock just below a wait-state boundary deliver more work than one just above it?
column2: Crossing the boundary adds a wait state to every missed branch target, so CPI jumps; the instruction rate \(f/\text{CPI}\) falls even though \(f\) rose.

column1: What do prefetch buffers and flash caches each recover?
column2: Prefetch of wide lines keeps straight-line code at full speed; a cache (or vendor accelerator) serves repeated branch targets such as loop bodies without a flash access.

column1: Why is race-to-idle optimal at the top of a wait-state band?
column2: Within a band CPI is constant, so energy falls as \(f\) rises (the fixed current is paid for less time); at each band edge CPI and energy jump up.

column1: Why does CoreMark/MHz overstate what a real MCU delivers?
column2: The published core figure assumes zero-wait-state memory; flash wait states, cache misses and the compiler reduce it, typically by several percent.

column1: What does a PLL configuration have to satisfy?
column2: The phase-detector input \(f_{in}/M\) and the VCO \(f_{in}N/M\) must lie in their ranges, and the output dividers \(P\), \(Q\) must give the system clock and an exact 48 MHz for USB if needed.

column1: Which sections go to flash and which to SRAM?
column2: Flash: .text (code, constants, vectors) and the initial values of .data. SRAM: .data, .bss, heap and stack. data therefore counts in both.

column1: What is the difference between load address and run address?
column2: .data is loaded (stored) in flash and runs from SRAM; startup code copies it from its load address (_sidata) to its run address (_sdata).

column1: What must startup code do before main?
column2: Set the stack pointer (the first vector word), copy .data from flash, zero .bss, set up clocks and the FPU if used, run C++ constructors, then call main.

column1: How do you change one field of a register without touching the others?
column2: Read, clear with \(\lnot M\) where \(M = (2^w - 1) \ll p\), OR in the new value shifted to \(p\), write back.

column1: Why does volatile not make a read-modify-write safe?
column2: It forces each access to happen but does not make the read-modify-write sequence atomic: an interrupt between the read and the write can change the register, and the write restores the stale copy.

column1: How do you make a read-modify-write safe against an interrupt handler?
column2: Make the writer that writes back the whole register atomic (a critical section masking the handler, or LDREX/STREX where supported), or have both contexts use set/clear registers so neither writes back a stale copy.

column1: Why might an optimizer delete a polling loop on a flag set by an interrupt?
column2: Without volatile the compiler may assume nothing else changes the flag, hoist the read out of the loop and turn it into an infinite loop or remove it.

column1: What does the linker script define?
column2: The memory regions (flash, SRAM), where each output section goes, its load and run addresses, symbols such as _etext, _edata, _ebss and _estack, and checks such as a stack-fits assertion.

column1: Registers, CMSIS or a vendor HAL: what does each trade?
column2: Direct registers: smallest and fastest, least portable. CMSIS: standard core access and register names. HAL: portability and speed of development at the cost of code size, latency and hidden behaviour.

column1: When is an interrupt better than polling?
column2: When events are rare or irregular and need a quick response: polling wastes CPU and adds latency up to its period; at very high event rates DMA beats both.

column1: What does the Cortex-M hardware do on exception entry?
column2: It stacks R0–R3, R12, LR, PC and xPSR, fetches the vector, and enters the handler with LR holding an EXC_RETURN value, so handlers can be plain C functions; tail-chaining skips unstacking between back-to-back handlers.

column1: How do group priority and subpriority differ?
column2: Only a more urgent group priority preempts a running handler; subpriority only orders pending requests of the same group.

column1: State the worst-case interrupt response-time recurrence.
column2: \(R_i = C_i + B_i + \sum_{j \in hp(i)}\lceil R_i/T_j\rceil C_j\), iterated from \(C_i + B_i\) until it converges or exceeds the deadline.

column1: What is blocking \(B_i\) in interrupt analysis?
column2: The longest time interrupt \(i\) cannot start although it is the most urgent request: a critical section with interrupts masked, or a lower-priority handler that cannot be preempted.

column1: Why use BASEPRI instead of PRIMASK for a critical section?
column2: BASEPRI masks only priorities at or below a threshold, so the most urgent handlers (which must not share the data) keep running and see no blocking.

column1: What fixes a timer's PWM frequency and resolution?
column2: \(f_{PWM} = f_{clk}/((PSC + 1)(ARR + 1))\); resolution is \(\log_2(f_{clk}/f_{PWM})\) bits with PSC = 0. Center-aligned mode costs one bit.

column1: How do you compute a period from two input-capture values on an \(n\)-bit timer?
column2: \((c_2 - c_1) \bmod 2^n\) ticks, done naturally with unsigned arithmetic of the counter's width; it is correct across one wrap only.

column1: How should a watchdog timeout be chosen?
column2: Above the longest healthy kick interval at the fastest oscillator; the longest timeout (slowest oscillator) is how long a hang lasts before reset.

column1: When does DMA pay?
column2: When data moves at a high, regular rate: it replaces one interrupt per item with one per block, cutting CPU load by the block size, at the cost of latency and memory.

column1: Ping-pong buffering: what condition makes a block size safe?
column2: \(L + a + bN \le N/f_s\), so \(N \ge (a + L)f_s/(1 - bf_s)\), which needs \(bf_s < 1\).

column1: With \(k \ge 3\) buffers, what two conditions must the block size meet?
column2: The deadline \(N \ge (a + L)f_s/((k - 1) - bf_s)\) and the throughput floor \(N \ge af_s/(1 - bf_s)\): extra buffers absorb latency but cannot make processing faster than arrival.

column1: What does a larger DMA block cost?
column2: Latency: a sample waits \(N/f_s\) for its block to fill plus the processing time, and memory grows as \(kN\).

column1: Estimate the CPU's slowdown from a DMA stream sharing its memory port.
column2: About \(p\rho\): the fraction of CPU cycles that access the port times the fraction the DMA occupies it. Putting DMA buffers in another SRAM bank removes it.

column1: How do you find the write position of a circular DMA buffer?
column2: head = (S − remaining count) mod S; unread bytes = (head − tail) mod S. The ring must hold everything that can arrive between two services.

column1: What goes wrong with DMA buffers on a core with a data cache?
column2: The CPU may read stale cached data, or invalidating a line shared with other variables discards their updates. Align buffers to the line size, pad to whole lines, clean before and invalidate after.

column1: What makes a single-producer, single-consumer ring buffer lock-free?
column2: Each side writes only its own index; with a power-of-two size and free-running unsigned indices, full is head − tail = S and empty is head = tail. Data must be visible before the index is published.

column1: How do you size an LED's series resistor on a GPIO pin?
column2: For the worst-case current, with the output at the rail: \(R \ge (V_{DD} - V_F)/I_{max}\), then the next standard value; check the package's total current limit.

column1: How is a UART's baud-rate divisor chosen with 16× oversampling?
column2: Divisor = \(f_{clk}/(16 \times \text{baud})\), rounded to an integer or to sixteenths for a fractional divisor; check the resulting error.

column1: What baud-rate mismatch does an 8N1 receiver with 16× oversampling tolerate?
column2: In theory the sender may be up to 5.26% slow or 4.58% fast (stop bit sampled at its centre, start detected within a sixteenth of a bit); aim for about ±2% total in practice.

column1: What limits SPI clock speed?
column2: The round trip: SCK output delay, trace delay, the target's clock-to-output and the trace back must fit, with the controller's setup time, in the time between launch and sampling (half a period in modes 0 and 3).

column1: How are I²C pull-ups bounded?
column2: Below by the sink current: \(R \ge (V_{DD} - V_{OL})/I_{OL}\). Above by the rise time: \(R \le t_r/(0.8473\,C_b)\) for the 30–70% rise.

column1: Why is I²C slow per useful byte?
column2: Each byte costs 9 clocks, and a register read needs address, register, repeated start and address again before the data; reading many bytes per transaction from a FIFO amortizes the overhead.

column1: Compare UART, SPI and I²C.
column2: UART: two wires, asynchronous, point to point. SPI: four wires plus a select per target, fastest, full duplex. I²C: two wires, addressed multi-drop, open drain, slow. I3C keeps two wires with push-pull speed.

column1: Open-drain versus push-pull outputs?
column2: Push-pull drives both levels and is fast; open-drain only pulls low, needs a pull-up, and allows wired-AND buses such as I²C and level shifting.

column1: Give an ideal ADC's LSB and SQNR.
column2: LSB = \(V_{REF}/2^N\); quantization noise LSB/√12; SQNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine. ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76)/6.02.

column1: How long must an ADC sample to settle to half an LSB?
column2: \(t_s \ge (N + 1)\tau\ln 2\) with \(\tau = (R_s + R_{sw})C_{sh}\): about 9 τ at 12 bits and 10.4 τ at 14 bits.

column1: What does an external capacitor at an ADC pin fix, and what does it not?
column2: It supplies the S/H's charge, so the sharing step is small if \(C_{ext} \ge C_{sh}(2^{N+1} - 1)\). It does not fix the DC error from refilling it through \(R_s\): the S/H looks like \(1/(fC_{sh})\).

column1: What is ratiometric measurement?
column2: Using the same supply as the sensor's excitation and the ADC's reference, so supply changes cancel in the code; with a fixed reference they appear as false readings.

column1: What can oversampling and averaging do?
column2: Reduce white noise by √M, gaining ½ log₂ M bits at 1/M the rate, provided there is enough noise to dither. They cannot remove INL, offset or a quantization error the noise never reveals.

column1: How does a PWM become a DAC, and at what cost?
column2: An RC low-pass averages it. One-LSB ripple needs \(\tau \ge 2^NT/4\), so bandwidth falls as \(4^{-N}\): each extra bit costs four times the bandwidth and settling time.

column1: What does a DAC's zero-order hold do to the spectrum?
column2: It multiplies by \(|\operatorname{sinc}(f/f_s)|\) (droop, −0.91 dB at \(f_s/4\), −3.92 dB at \(f_s/2\)) and leaves images at \(kf_s \pm f\) that a reconstruction filter must remove.

column1: Why does the ADC reference matter as much as the converter?
column2: Every code is a ratio to \(V_{REF}\): its tolerance, drift and noise appear directly in the result, so a 1% reference error is about 41 LSB near full scale at 12 bits.

column1: What does an RTOS give you over a superloop?
column2: Preemptive priorities so urgent work runs on time regardless of other code, blocking primitives instead of polling, and structure; at the cost of stacks per task, kernel overhead and concurrency bugs.

column1: State the Liu & Layland bound.
column2: Independent periodic tasks with implicit deadlines on one core are RM-schedulable if \(U \le n(2^{1/n} - 1)\): 0.828 for two, 0.780 for three, → ln 2. Sufficient, not necessary.

column1: What is the hyperbolic bound?
column2: RM-schedulable if \(\prod(1 + U_i) \le 2\): never worse than Liu & Layland, still only sufficient.

column1: When does EDF beat RM?
column2: EDF schedules any implicit-deadline set with U ≤ 1 on one core; RM can fail above its bound, as with (2, 5) and (4, 7).

column1: What is unbounded priority inversion?
column2: A high-priority task waits for a mutex held by a low one, which is preempted by unrelated medium tasks, so the high task's delay grows with the medium tasks' work.

column1: Priority inheritance versus priority ceiling?
column2: Inheritance raises the holder to the waiter's priority when blocking occurs; immediate ceiling raises it on locking. Ceiling blocks a task at most once and prevents deadlock; inheritance can chain.

column1: How many slots must a queue have?
column2: Enough for everything produced during the consumer's longest stall: \(\lfloor t_{stall}/T\rfloor + 1\), counting arrivals at both ends.

column1: Where does RTOS RAM go?
column2: Each task's stack and control block, queues and kernel objects. Stacks dominate and must be sized for the worst call depth plus interrupt stacking.

column1: Why measure stack usage instead of guessing?
column2: Overflow corrupts neighbouring memory silently; fill stacks with a pattern and check the high-water mark, use the MPU or stack limit registers to trap overflow.

column1: What does a bootloader do at reset?
column2: Chooses a valid image, verifies its integrity and signature, handles a pending update (swap, copy or revert), then jumps to the application's vector table.

column1: Single slot versus two slots?
column2: A single slot gives the largest image but no good copy during an update unless a recovery bootloader exists; two slots halve the image size but always keep a bootable image.

column1: Why must an update be confirmed?
column2: A new image that boots but misbehaves is reverted automatically unless the application confirms it after its own health checks: the test-then-confirm pattern.

column1: What makes a swap update power-fail safe?
column2: Every step is recorded in flash so the bootloader can resume after a cut; status writes must be atomic and the resume rule must match every intermediate state.

column1: What does secure boot cost?
column2: Hashing the image (cycles per byte × size) plus one signature check at every boot; a hash engine leaves the signature dominant.

column1: What is anti-rollback protection?
column2: A monotonic security counter (often fuses) that refuses older images with known vulnerabilities; increment it only for security-relevant releases, because fuses run out.

column1: What do delta updates trade?
column2: Smaller downloads (airtime, energy, cost, exposure to link drops) for patching code, working space and a patch per installed version on the server.

column1: What is the scratch area's wear problem?
column2: A swap through one scratch sector erases it once per image sector per update, so its endurance limits the number of updates; swap-using-move avoids it.

column1: How do you compute a duty-cycled device's average current?
column2: Sum the charge of each active phase plus sleep current over the rest of the period, divided by the period. Battery life = usable capacity / average current.

column1: When does a deeper sleep mode pay?
column2: When the idle time exceeds the extra wake-up charge divided by the current it saves: \(t > \Delta Q/(I_{shallow} - I_{deep})\).

column1: Why does race-to-idle usually win at fixed voltage?
column2: The dynamic charge per task is the same at any clock; the fixed current is paid per unit time, so finishing sooner saves it.

column1: When can running slower beat racing?
column2: When the lower clock allows a lower core voltage, which cuts dynamic energy (∝ V² at the core, ∝ V in battery charge through an LDO) by more than the extra fixed current costs.

column1: LDO or buck for a low-power product?
column2: A buck draws less battery current at load, because it converts voltage rather than burning the difference; an LDO has lower quiescent current and no ripple; many PMICs use the buck when active and the LDO in sleep.

column1: Why does a coin cell brown out on a radio burst?
column2: Its internal resistance (higher when cold or discharged) drops \(IR\); a reservoir capacitor supplies the burst, with droop \(IR(1 - e^{-t/RC})\).

column1: What usually dominates a product's sleep current?
column2: Often the board, not the chip: dividers across the battery, enabled references, pull-ups and leaking peripherals.

column1: What is energy-neutral operation for a harvester?
column2: Over the worst period of the year, harvested energy must cover consumption plus storage losses, with storage sized for the longest dark stretch.

column1: How does a MEMS accelerometer measure acceleration?
column2: A proof mass on springs deflects \(x = a/\omega_0^2\), changing differential capacitances by \(2x/d\); electronics read the imbalance.

column1: What sets a MEMS accelerometer's mechanical noise floor?
column2: Brownian motion of the proof mass: \(\sqrt{4k_BT\omega_0/(mQ)}\) per √Hz, lower for a heavier mass and higher Q.

column1: How do you turn a noise density into rms noise?
column2: Multiply by √B for a brick-wall bandwidth B (one-sided density); real filters need their noise bandwidth.

column1: How does a vibratory gyroscope sense rotation?
column2: A mass is driven at resonance; rotation Ω produces a Coriolis acceleration \(2\Omega v\) perpendicular to the drive velocity, sensed as a tiny deflection.

column1: Angle random walk from a rate noise density?
column2: With the one-sided density ρ in °/s/√Hz, \(\sigma_\theta = \rho\sqrt{t/2}\) and ARW = \(60\rho/\sqrt2\) °/√h; check the data sheet's convention, since the shortcut 60ρ is off by √2.

column1: Why does gyroscope bias matter more than noise over minutes?
column2: Bias integrates linearly (bt) while noise grows as √t: 0.5 °/s of bias is 30° after a minute.

column1: What does a complementary filter do?
column2: It high-passes the integrated gyroscope and low-passes the accelerometer tilt with time constant \(\alpha\Delta t/(1 - \alpha)\); bias error \(b\tau\), noise passed \(\sqrt{(1 - \alpha)/(1 + \alpha)}\).

column1: What limits PPG heart-rate accuracy on the wrist?
column2: Motion artefacts and perfusion, far more than shot noise; the LED duty cycle is the power lever.

column1: Microphone sensitivity −26 dBFS: what does it mean?
column2: A 94 dB SPL (1 Pa) tone gives −26 dBFS, so full scale is 120 dB SPL; noise floor = 94 − SNR in dB SPL.

column1: What are the parts of a threat model?
column2: Assets worth protecting, attackers with their capabilities and budgets, and attack surfaces; then the countermeasures each pair justifies.

column1: What is a root of trust and a chain of trust?
column2: Immutable boot code and keys that verify the next stage, which verifies the next, so every executing image is authenticated back to the root.

column1: What does TrustZone-M provide?
column2: Hardware separation of Secure and Non-secure worlds on Armv8-M, with calls through secure gateways; Secure code must check that pointers it receives refer to Non-secure memory.

column1: Why does an early-exit comparison leak a secret?
column2: Its time depends on how many leading bytes match, so an attacker can recover the secret byte by byte with about 256 × repetitions queries per byte.

column1: How many traces does a CPA need?
column2: About \((z/\rho)^2\), with \(\rho = \sqrt{2/(2 + \sigma^2)}\) for Hamming-weight leakage of a byte; at high noise \(N \approx z^2\sigma^2/2\).

column1: Why does masking defeat first-order side-channel attacks?
column2: A fresh random mask makes the processed value uniform whatever the key, so its leakage is uncorrelated with any key guess; second-order attacks remain.

column1: Why do PUF keys need error correction?
column2: Each cell flips with some probability, and a 128-bit key needs all bits right: at 3% per cell a raw key is correct only 2% of the time.

column1: Why does duplicating a security check help against glitching?
column2: Independent faults must succeed twice, squaring the probability; the checks must be complementary, separated and not merged by the compiler.

column1: What is the honeypot argument?
column2: A key shared across a fleet makes one extraction compromise every device, dividing the attack cost by the fleet size; per-device keys keep it per device.

column1: What does the EU Cyber Resilience Act require of MCU-based products?
column2: Security by design, vulnerability handling over a support period of at least five years unless the product's life is shorter, and reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities (early warning within 24 hours).
